rationale: Large, well-powered field experiment plus online study; preregistered, IRB-approved, administrative outcomes, careful design, and mechanism probing. Estimates are credible and policy-relevant. Limits: collaboration only with opposition partners, one partisan arm, potential spillovers, and uncertain availability of full replication materials; external validity beyond Türkiye is open. Overall ranks in the top decile of recent political economy field experiments.

Main claims (widespread misperceptions; accurate information shifts beliefs and votes) are clearly stated and supported by convergent online and field evidence. Placebo controls mitigate demand effects; heterogeneity aligns with mechanism theory. Authors are cautious in scope. Minor caveat: longer-run effect is marginal; mechanism causality relies on heterogeneity rather than dedicated manipulation.

Neighborhood-level randomization, strong first stages, 2SLS on compliance, administrative outcomes, robustness checks, and an online placebo design; preregistered and IRB-cleared. Threats (interference, partisan implementation, minor imbalance) discussed and largely addressed; SUTVA untestable. Multiple-election replication strengthens credibility. Formal multiple-testing adjustments are not emphasized.

Rare, large-scale causal evidence that correcting institutional misperceptions can shift votes under authoritarianism. Integrates online and field experiments, examining messenger credibility and targeting the misinformed. Moves debate beyond polarization-only effects. External validity to other settings/issues is uncertain, but contribution is substantive.

Questions and theory are explicit; assumptions transparent; analyses and robustness are clearly presented. Figures/tables support the narrative and results are cautiously interpreted. Complexity from bundled/unbundled treatments and multiple panels may tax readers, but the reasoning remains coherent and consistent.

IRB approvals and AEA RCT registration; instruments and OSM shared; outcomes use public administrative data. It is unclear if full code, randomization files, and canvassing logs are publicly posted; some microdata may be restricted. Replication appears feasible but may not be fully turnkey.

Highly relevant to democracy support under authoritarianism, with practical guidance on information content, messenger credibility, and targeting. Timely, scalable insights and quantified electoral impacts inform policy and civil society strategies. Implementation depends on local legal and ethical constraints.

Influential, well-argued theory paper that frames key AI–growth mechanisms (automation, Baumol effects, idea production) and offers clear agendas. Limited empirical validation and open-science practices temper the score, as do strong simplifying assumptions (exogenous automation). Still highly relevant to policy and research, with strong exposition and conceptual contributions.

Main claims are posed as questions and cautiously characterized; evidence is primarily theoretical with illustrative simulations and sectoral facts. Authors discuss limitations (e.g., exogenous automation, bottlenecks, business-stealing) and alternative mechanisms. Empirical support is light and non-identifying, so claims remain partially speculative by design.

Clean extensions of Zeira and task-based CES frameworks; transparent neoclassical closure and simulations. Assumptions are reasonable for agenda-setting but automation is exogenous; robustness explored qualitatively across parameter regimes. No causal empirics or formal calibration/estimation; limited sensitivity analysis.

Integrates Baumol’s cost disease with automation, clarifies conditions for balanced growth vs acceleration, and formalizes singularity scenarios. Helped shape subsequent research on AI and growth. Practical guidance is high-level; limited quantification reduces immediate applied impact.

Questions and assumptions are explicit; reasoning is coherent and transparent. Models are clearly laid out; conclusions match derivations. Writing is accessible and effective for economists and policymakers. Minor reliance on stylized setups does not detract from clarity.

No replication package or code provided; uses public data sources but limited documentation for simulations. Methods are reproducible in principle for theory but empirical sections are not turnkey. Not preregistered; no multiple-testing issues relevant.

Addresses globally salient topics: AI’s effects on growth, labor shares, inequality, market structure. Policy implications (competition, IP, organization) are discussed, though quantification is limited and LMIC-specific analysis is brief. High relevance for priority-setting and foresight.

Overall reflects the mean across categories. Strong saturation-RCT design, clear empirical results, and policy relevance. Credibility is high but tempered by some measurement limitations (imprecise denominators in a subset of villages, retrospective employer outcomes), limited multiple-testing adjustments, and external-validity concerns given later mixed scale-up evidence.

Main claims—subsidies raise migration; spillovers increase village wages/hours; limited food price effects—are well supported by a saturation RCT, strong first stages, high-frequency household data, and employer/price surveys. Some secondary claims (employer profits, specific prices) are weaker due to retrospective measures and imprecise denominators in some villages. External validity is cautioned.

Well-justified saturation design enabling GE identification; IV with strong first stages; high-frequency measurement reduces recall bias; clustered SEs; checks on spatial spillovers. Assumptions (closed labor markets, short-run technology rigidity) are reasonable but not airtight. Limited multiple-hypothesis adjustments and some retrospective modules reduce robustness.

Provides rare experimental evidence on GE spillovers of internal migration, documenting wage, labor-supply, and distributional effects. Influential for debates on mobility policies and program scale-up. Incremental relative to more recent GE work and context-specific; later mixed results at scale temper field-wide impact.

Clear questions and theory organizing empirics; transparent assumptions; consistent logic from first stage to GE outcomes; coherent triangulation across HF surveys, endline, employers, and prices. Tables/labels are clear; limitations acknowledged.

Pre-registered (AEA RCT registry 2507) with disclosures and substantial design detail. Public data/code availability is unclear; complex implementation may hinder easy reproduction; limited explicit multiple-testing plans. Better than average pre-2019 standards, below current best practices.

Highly relevant to LMIC policy on seasonal hunger, internal migration, and rural labor markets; quantifies wage and price effects useful to practitioners. Applicability varies with context and market integration; later scale-up evidence mixed, warranting cautious extrapolation.

Rounded mean of component midpoints. Excellent causal design and scale; strong online evidence and useful policy takeaways. Uncertainty stems from limited offline behavioral results and constraints on data sharing/replication.

Core questions are clear; endorsement and source-citation effects identified causally with platform-specific variation. Offline impacts are framed as suggestive and caveated. Evidence is strong for online diffusion; offline outcomes rely on survey measures with selection and self-report limits.

Large preregistered field experiment; clever identification exploiting Twitter’s author/retweeter visibility. Robustness via forced-retweet randomization and checks on visible engagement counts; appropriate Poisson models and fixed effects. Assumptions reasonable. Limited power for offline behavior; external validity beyond Twitter/users is constrained.

Provides rare causal separation of endorsement vs reach at national scale; shows source citation can hinder diffusion; informs complex contagion shape. High practical and theoretical relevance for social influence and health communication. Offline behavior effects are limited, tempering the ceiling.
Goals, design, and assumptions are explicit; reasoning links evidence to claims cleanly. Figures/tables align with narrative; caveats stated. Dense in places but overall very clear and transparent.

Pre-registered; IRB approved; methods and analyses described in detail. Twitter data likely restricted by TOS; code/data availability not fully open, and platform changes hinder reproduction. Still, procedures are documented enough for credible replication in similar contexts.

Directly relevant to vaccine promotion and public communications in LMICs; offers actionable guidance on influencer use, messaging, sources, and exposure strategy. Quantifies effects useful for campaign design; downstream behavioral evidence is modest.

Strong theoretical contribution plus solid empirical demonstrations; some external-validity and assumption limits temper the score. Results are decision-relevant and clearly communicated. Average across categories reasonably reflects performance; no single metric dominates enough to override the default mean.

Clear questions and claims; theory tightly linked to empirics. Two incentivized RCTs estimate ATEs, heterogeneity, and covariance with bias/externalities. Sensitivity analyses (pass-through, markups, variance/covariance) aid credibility. Limits: cars choices are hypothetical; drinks bias relies on proxies; key independence/normality assumptions; external validity cautions.

Rigorous sufficient-statistic framework with Weyl–Fabinger supply; careful mapping to estimands. Mixed-effects estimation of Var[τ] via dispersion, and targeting via Cov with bias/externalities. Preregistration, incentivization, and extensive sensitivity. Weaknesses: no PAP, normality/independence assumptions, proxy-based bias in drinks, non-naturalistic car choices, literature-based pass-through.

Shifts nudge evaluation from average effects to distortion-variance and targeting; unifies taxes, pass-through, market power, psychic costs. Portable sufficient statistics; dual experiments illustrate feasibility. Likely to influence behavioral public finance and policy appraisal.

Goals and assumptions explicit; derivations and intuition (examples, figures) are clear. Empirical-to-theory mapping is transparent. Caveats and limitations are candid. Minor complexity remains for non-specialists.

Trials registered (AEA, ClinicalTrials); IRB approvals; replication files posted. Methods sufficiently detailed for reproduction. No full pre-analysis plan; some data access constraints (panel, shipping logistics). Overall, above-average transparency.

High policy relevance (labels, sin taxes, nudges) across sectors; guidance on when nudges help or harm welfare, useful for regulators and practitioners. Empirics are US-centric; limited direct cost/practical implementation detail for LMIC contexts, but framework generalizes.

Strong causal identification and extensive robustness yield credible, decision-relevant results disentangling knowledge, people, and patents. Communication is clear; practical implications are meaningful. Uncertainty remains around exclusion restrictions for the IVs and generalizability beyond the U.S. context. Open-science practices are moderate. Overall quality is high among recent applied-innovation studies.

Core claims (people positive, university patents crowd out, publications per se limited) are clearly stated and consistently supported across outcomes, specifications, and robustness checks (alternative IVs, Poisson CF, heterogeneity, invention quality). Evidence characterization is cautious. Remaining concerns: possible residual violations of exclusion restrictions and interpretation of Tobin’s Q channel.

Thoughtful firm-level shift-share IVs using predicted agency R&D from appropriations subcommittee composition; strong first stages; multiple alternative instruments; careful construction of relevance via CPC/OECD and SPECTER; extensive sensitivity/heterogeneity analyses; IV-Poisson for counts. Assumptions are explicit. Residual risks: Bartik identifying assumptions and potential political-economy confounds.

Novel decomposition of public science into knowledge, human capital, and invention at the firm level; clarifies channels and heterogeneity (frontier vs followers; industries). Results challenge common spillover narratives and inform policy on university commercialization and PhD training. Substantial contribution to innovation economics; some limits to external validity beyond U.S. institutions.

Clear motivation, framework, data description, and econometric setup. Logical flow from theory to empirics; assumptions and limitations discussed. Figures/tables integrate with narrative. Minor complexity in instrument construction may challenge some readers; some interpretations (e.g., value effects) could be further unpacked.

Uses multiple large external datasets; DISCERN dataset link provided; detailed appendices. However, full replication likely requires proprietary data (Dimensions, ProQuest) and code availability is unclear. Reproducibility is credible for those with access but not fully open. Documentation quality is good.

High policy relevance for science/innovation funding, tech transfer, and workforce training. Insights likely generalize qualitatively, but identification and institutional mechanisms are U.S.-specific (appropriations, Bayh–Dole). Practical guidance for incumbents and universities is evident; cost/benefit quantification for interventions is indirect.

Overall reflects the mean of category scores. Strong causal identification and policy relevance; careful presentation and triangulation. Open-science limitations and some residual identification assumptions (rain-based RVI, monotonicity, external validity) slightly temper the score.

Clear statement of the question; precise causal claims focused on LATE; multiple robustness checks (placebos, dynamics, panel corroboration). Evidence convincingly supports increased firm creation. Some residual concerns remain about formalization vs. new entry, compliers’ representativeness, and possible alternative channels.

Novel, well-argued running-variable instrument with fuzzy RD/IV; strong first stage; balance and profiling; permutation-based expected instrument; complementary panel DiD. Assumptions (rain exogeneity within week×location, monotonicity, no direct effects) are plausible but nontrivial; administrative matching noise possible.

First rigorous estimate (to my knowledge) of legalization’s impact on entrepreneurship in a developing-country context; adds practice-relevant magnitudes and a reusable method. External validity beyond Venezuelans in Colombia is uncertain but the contribution is substantive.

Reasoning is transparent; assumptions and design laid out carefully; results tied to claims with clear narrative and figures. Technical sections are dense, which may challenge some readers, but overall argumentation is coherent and consistent.

Uses administrative data unlikely to be publicly shareable; methods and appendices are detailed, but no explicit code/data repository is indicated. Replication feasible in principle with access, but practical reproducibility is constrained.

Highly relevant to migration regularization policies and entrepreneurship in LMICs; produces actionable effect sizes and timing. Findings inform integration strategies and institutional design; generalizability plausible though context-specific factors remain.

Exceptionally strong, policy-relevant RCT with novel UBI design and careful analysis. Major strengths: scale, pre-registration, multiple arms, high compliance, rich outcomes, and clear caveats. Limitations: short time horizon so far, modest power for cross-arm contrasts and prices, some self-reports, and external validity beyond rural Kenya. Overall score equals mean of component midpoints.

Clear questions (UBI vs short-term vs lump-sum), strong multi-source evidence (household, enterprise census, wages, prices), and cautious interpretation. Authors pre-specify aggregates, acknowledge limited power for between-arm two-sided tests and uncertain price effects, and align findings with a simple model without overstating causality on mechanisms.

Large village-level RCT; strong pre-registration; high response and compliance; migrant tracking; Conley SEs; multiple data modules. Sensible specification choices and transparency on limits. Limits: between-arm power constraints, short-run horizon, some self-reported measures, and limited ability to identify general-equilibrium price effects.

First large UBI RCT with 12-year commitment and cross-arm modality contrasts. Provides rare evidence on structural shifts, occupational choice, enterprise dynamics, mental health, and the importance of tranching and duration. Highly influential for cash-transfer design and understanding savings/credit constraints in LMICs.

Objectives, concepts, and assumptions are explicit; theory-to-empirics link is clear. Writing is thorough and transparent about caveats and inference limits. Tables and figures generally match narrative and are interpretable; minor density/complexity is expected given scope.

Pre-analysis plan registered; IRBs and conflicts disclosed; design and measures well-documented. Replication seems feasible, but public availability of full data/code isn’t clearly established in the text provided; hence a conservative score pending confirmed open materials.

Directly relevant to UBI and cash-transfer policy in LMICs under fiscal and administrative constraints. Results inform modality (lump-sum vs streams), duration, and macro spillovers for practitioners. Communication is accessible for policymakers, with quantitative magnitudes and practical implications.

Strengths in clarity and high policy relevance offset by reliance on modeling assumptions, moderate methodological novelty, and limited openness. Overall reflects the mean of sub-scores; decisions hinge on simulated evidence with good sensitivity checks but uncertain replicability.

Main questions and claims are clear: portfolio economics for mRNA EID vaccines are unattractive without public support. Evidence is simulation-based, calibrated to literature and expert input, with extensive sensitivity analyses. Characterization of limitations is generally accurate, though some strong conclusions hinge on uncertain price/demand assumptions.

Monte Carlo framework with correlated trial outcomes, outbreak stochasticity, cost models, and sensitivity analysis is reasonable. The biologically motivated correlation metric is plausible but unvalidated; many parameters are assumed. No preregistration or code shown; no multiple-testing issues but model risk remains. Robustness explored but empirical validation is limited.

Extends prior megafund work by adding mRNA-specific parameters, outbreak-driven cash flows, and clearer cost/revenue drivers (e.g., price-per-dose threshold, clinical cost dominance). Useful for policy design, but advances are incremental and depend on assumptions; limited direct empirical contribution.

Well-structured, transparent about assumptions, clear executive summary and visuals. Reasoning links methods to conclusions coherently; sensitivity analyses support claims. Some parameter choices could use deeper justification, but overall argumentation is easy to follow and consistent.

Parameters are sourced and supplementary materials are referenced, but code/data availability is unclear. Replication would be straightforward with code, yet not evidently provided. No preregistration. Internal consistency appears solid, but openness and reproducibility practices seem limited.

Highly relevant to pandemic preparedness, vaccine financing, and policy tools (AMCs, stockpiles, guarantees). Addresses practical constraints (affordability, cannibalization, trial costs) and offers decision-relevant thresholds. Findings are actionable for governments, funders, and CEPI-like entities.

Well-executed RCT with credible short-term impacts on mental health and skills, strong policy relevance, and clear exposition. Limitations: short follow-up, reliance on self-reports for key outcomes, and modest open-science practices. Percentile reflects balanced strengths across categories.

Main claims are clearly stated and largely supported by experimental evidence and predictive heterogeneity. The two-pathways mechanism is plausible but partly identified; economic outcomes are proxied and short-term. No long-run evidence; several outcomes are self-reported. Strong but not definitive.

Clustered RCT with re-randomization, baseline controls, randomization inference, indices, and LASSO with holdout for heterogeneity—appropriate and transparent. Risks: many outcomes without formal FWER/FDR beyond indices, short horizon, unclear preregistration, and possible reporting bias.

Shows sizeable short-run impacts of group CBT by lay counselors in a general poor population; challenges targeting-only view; introduces predictive vulnerability heterogeneity. Adds to development and global mental health literatures with a practical delivery model. Lacks long-run and cost-effectiveness estimates.

Clear framing and theory (bandwidth, vulnerability), design, and results; limitations and contrast with Kenyan null are discussed. Reasoning is mostly transparent; some mechanistic claims remain interpretive. Presentation appears coherent and consistent.
Manual shared and methods described; RI and LASSO details provided. However, no explicit public posting of data/code or preregistration is indicated, limiting ease of replication and reuse.

Addresses mental health and human capital in a low-income setting with a scalable delivery model (NSS-compatible), showing meaningful short-run gains. High policy salience. Practical usefulness would increase with costs, implementation detail, and durability evidence.

Overall equals the mean of the six category midpoints. Strengths in clarity and practical guidance; moderate originality and limited formal robustness checks or open tools keep the score below top-tier. Uncertainty is higher given limited visibility into full implementation details.

Main questions (Type M/S errors; external validity of RCTs) are explicit. Evidence is conceptual and literature-based, with a worked example; claims are generally calibrated and caveats noted. Limited new empirical testing constrains strength of evidence.

Applies established statistical ideas (Type M/S, discounting) to CEA with reasonable assumptions. Robustness is discussed qualitatively; little formal sensitivity analysis, preregistration, or multiple-testing correction (mostly not applicable for a guide). Validity hinges on careful interpretation rather than new estimation.

Synthesizes dispersed concepts into actionable guidance for CEA practitioners, likely improving practice by tempering overinterpretation and misgeneralization. Contribution is primarily integrative and pedagogical; limited novel methodology or parameter estimates.

Clear structure (summary, key takeaways, guidance, worked example). Concepts defined and reasoning steps explicit; conclusions aligned with presented arguments. Minor quantitative thresholds could use fuller derivations, but overall communication is strong and practitioner-friendly.

As a conceptual guide, data/code are not central. Citations and reasoning appear transparent; reproducibility of the worked example likely. However, limited provision of reusable code, datasets, or formal replication materials reduces the open-science score.

Directly relevant to cost-effectiveness analysis in global health/development and philanthropy. Guidance on discounting noisy evidence and generalization is actionable for analysts and decision-makers, supporting better allocation under uncertainty.

Arithmetic mean of category midpoints. Strong RCTs with long-run follow-up, robust results on mental health and behavioral updating; transparent nulls on economics. Open-science practices are good but not exemplary.

Clear questions; two randomized trials with 4–5 year follow-up. Strong, well-powered effects for HAP; transparent nulls for THPP and economic outcomes. Expert-forecast benchmarking adds credibility. Limitations and deviations from PAP are disclosed and minor.

Credible RCT design; balanced attrition; validated PHQ-9; incentivized tasks; DML controls; multiple-hypothesis corrections; robustness and mediation analyses. Limits: 24–31% attrition, limited power for some outcomes, some modules added post-PAP, external validity constraints.

Major contribution on long-run psychotherapy impacts in LMICs; cost-effectiveness quantified; novel evidence on belief updating and self-perception; recalibrates expert priors; clarifies limits on economic outcomes, guiding complementary interventions.
Goals, concepts, and assumptions are clear. Argument flows logically; analyses match claims; nulls and caveats are explicit. Tables/figures are interpretable; consistency across sections is strong.

IRB, preregistration, and pre-analysis plan; multiple-hypothesis adjustments; expert forecasts via SSPP. Replication seems feasible, but public data/code availability is unclear/limited due to human-subject constraints.

High policy relevance for mental health scale-up in LMICs; durable, low-cost effects; quantified cost per depression-month averted. Practical insights on lack of economic gains inform program design and integration with other supports.

Overall set to the mean of component midpoints. Clear, persuasive synthesis with actionable proposals, but causal evidence is limited and open-science practices are weak. Strong communication and relevance raise the score; methods and evidentiary strength are closer to median relative to recent science-of-science work.

Main claim—citation-centric incentives reduce exploration and contribute to stagnation—is supported by a conceptual model, illustrative case studies (PCR, CRISPR), descriptive bibliometrics, and related literature. However, causal identification is limited, biomedicine-heavy, and robustness is modest. Characterization of evidence is mostly fair but occasionally overreaches on causality.

Uses a simple lifecycle model and a text-based novelty metric (UMLS concept vintage) with descriptive analyses. Reasonable and transparent, but lacks causal identification, pre-registration, and extensive sensitivity checks. Replicable in principle but dependent on proprietary data and not fully specified for exact reproduction.

Advances the policy conversation by foregrounding novelty metrics (“edge factors”) alongside impact and by linking incentives to exploration. Adds synthesis and practical recommendations more than new empirical breakthroughs. Contribution is useful and timely, though overlapping with concurrent science-of-science literature.

Clear framing, definitions, and argument flow; figures clarify the lifecycle thesis. Reasoning is largely transparent with apt examples. Some causal claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, but overall communication quality is high.

No evident shared code/data; relies on PubMed/Web of Science with limited reproducibility detail. No preregistration, limited robustness materials, and no replication package. Methods are described but not to the level enabling straightforward reanalysis.

Highly relevant to funders, universities, and policymakers concerned with research productivity worldwide. Recommendations (dual metrics; search engine changes) are actionable, though implementation challenges and cost-benefit quantification are not deeply developed.

Overall reflects the mean of sub-scores. The paper is conceptually interesting and clearly presented, but empirical support is weak due to hypothetical elicitation issues, extreme skew/outliers, small effective sample sizes, and sensitivity to researcher decisions. Policy relevance is high but evidence quality limits confidence.

Main questions are explicit and results reported transparently. However, claims about magnitudes (e.g., welfare costs exceeding climate costs) rest on highly hypothetical WTP/WTA with extreme skew, small N after exclusions, and strong sensitivity to outlier handling. External validity is limited (Belgium-only). Authors acknowledge many limitations, but some abstract statements are stronger than warranted.

Uses contingent valuation with a novel ‘pill’ scenario, cheap talk, certainty scales, randomization, and comprehension checks; applies nonparametric tests and sensitivity analyses. Yet heavy attrition, ex post exclusion rules, extreme outliers, lack of preregistration/multiplicity controls, small sample, and epistemically transformative content undermine validity and robustness.

Introduces and operationalizes a non-anthropocentric SWF with representative-agent WTP/WTA for animal welfare, linking to optimal taxation and cross-externality concerns. Provides first-cut estimates and comparisons to prior modeling work. Despite weak empirics, the conceptual framing can stimulate better-designed follow-ups.

Clear motivation and theoretical setup; assumptions are mostly explicit; limitations and sensitivity are candidly discussed. Some overreach between evidence and conclusions; complex exclusions/outlier handling can confuse. Tables generally align with narrative.

No preregistration, data, or code availability indicated. Survey instrument only partially reproduced. Outlier and winsorization choices are described but not fully auditable without materials. Replication would be approximate rather than exact.

Topic (animal welfare externalities, meat taxation, cross-externality trade-offs) is globally salient for policy and prioritization. Findings could inform debates (e.g., chicken vs beef). Generalizability is limited by the Belgian sample and hypothetical method, but practical relevance remains notable.

Exceptional large-scale RCT with clear mechanisms and GE tests; claims are well supported and policy-relevant. Minor deductions for open-science limitations and context-specificity. Overall reflects the mean of component scores.

Main questions are explicit; evidence is strong: nationwide firm-level RCT, cross-randomized intensity, and appeal-level visibility experiment. Effects on violations, emissions, regulator behavior, and ambient SO2 triangulate. Alternative mechanisms probed and largely ruled out. External validity is the main caveat.

Well-justified design; preregistered; firm FE, province×day FE, appropriate clustering, event studies, alternative definitions, manipulation checks, and GE design. Appealing identification at scale. Some multiple-testing risk and a few appeal-level analyses are cross-sectional, but overall robustness is high.

First experimental evidence at national scale on citizen participation’s direct and indirect effects in environmental governance; identifies regulator responsiveness via social media visibility. Influential for political economy and policy design. Generalizability beyond China is uncertain but insights are substantial.

Clear goals, concepts, and transparent reasoning. Results logically support conclusions; figures/tables align with narrative. Length and technical density may limit accessibility for some practitioners, but exposition is careful and accurate.

AEA RCT registry and detailed appendices/protocols. However, core administrative data are not fully public; code/materials availability is not fully clear, limiting turnkey replication. Documentation quality is good given constraints.

High relevance to environmental governance, accountability, and cost-effective compliance tools in LMICs. Actionable insights for regulators/NGOs. Institutional features (CEMS scale, Chinese social media) may limit direct transfer, but principles generalize well.

Overall quality is strong: clear question, careful experimental design, robust analysis, and practical implications. Limits include stated-preference nature, modest response rate, and incomplete openness. The midpoint equals the mean of the six category midpoints; no single metric dominates decision relevance.

Claims are clear and appropriately bounded: scientists value dissensus (variance), experts more so; bimodality not preferred; tighter budgets reduce tolerance; potential funding reversals. Evidence: two well-powered DCEs with NIH-funded scientists, randomized proposal proximity, multiple robustness checks, and application to external datasets. Main caveats: stated preferences not revealed behavior, selection/response bias, and no preregistration.

Strong DCE design (BIBD), randomized expertise proximity, fixed effects, clustered SEs, multinomial and G-MNL robustness, and placebo/hover checks. Sensible modeling of score moments and heterogeneity. Limits: hypothetical choices, potential multiple-testing without formal adjustment, modest attention verification, and external validity to real funding outcomes.

Provides quantitative evidence that variance (dissensus) contains valued information and that experts are more tolerant; budgets matter asymmetrically. Offers actionable insight for funding rules and tie-breaking. Contribution is meaningful but incremental within science-of-science literature; does not establish causal effects of alternative aggregation on scientific impact.

Well-structured and transparent. Clear exposition of NIH context, experimental design, estimation, robustness, and limits. Results logically follow from analyses; figures/tables support narrative. Claims are nuanced and consistent with evidence.

Data appendix provided; methods described in detail. However, it is unclear if full de-identified data and code are publicly available; no preregistration noted. Replication appears feasible but not turnkey. Some constraints may stem from confidentiality of participants and prior datasets.

High relevance for funders worldwide (NIH, NSF, philanthropies) considering reforms to peer-review aggregation. Offers practical guidance (use of variance, tie-breaking), with quantified potential reversals. Implementation requires piloting and context-specific validation; benefits span many research areas and countries.

Overall quality is strong: clear questions, sound methods, careful comparisons, and policy-relevant conclusions. Main weaknesses are limited open-science practices and reliance on U.S. context with some measurement constraints. Score equals the mean of component midpoints.

Research questions are explicit and the central claim—severity proxies outperform infection counts for long-run outcomes—is well supported. Predictive checks validate the epidemiological model for outbreaks; reduced-form estimates are robust and transparently contrasted. Limitations (age-missing case data, mortality as severity proxy) are acknowledged and evidence is characterized appropriately.

Methodology is well-justified: SIR-based accounting with reporting-rate estimation, sensitivity analyses, and reduced-form designs with fixed effects and clustered SEs. Assumptions are reasonable and tested. Constraints include national (not state) vaccination rollout data, age-agnostic infection allocation, no preregistration, and limited multiple-testing adjustments.

The paper advances understanding by directly comparing epidemiological accounting with reduced-form approaches and highlighting disease severity’s importance for long-run human capital. It refines methodological guidance rather than introducing a new identification strategy; complements contemporaneous work (e.g., Atwood 2022) with clear implications for applied research.

Argumentation is clear and coherent; assumptions and steps are explicit; validations and robustness checks are logically tied to claims. Narrative is easy to follow and conclusions remain aligned with presented evidence. Presentation quality is high.

Uses publicly available datasets, but there is no explicit replication package or code release noted. Methods are described sufficiently for careful replication, yet effort would be nontrivial. Data provenance is clear; reusable outputs (e.g., cohort infection shares) are not evidently shared.

Highly relevant to vaccination policy and prioritization; emphasizes benefits where disease severity is high, aligning with LMIC priorities. However, empirical evidence is U.S.-based and lacks explicit cost-effectiveness metrics, limiting immediate operational applicability across settings.
Arithmetic mean of the six category midpoints. Strong global relevance and careful modeling are offset by reliance on subjective forecasts and uncertain open-science practices.

Two clear core questions, transparent quantitative model integrating income and health, and use of historical growth evidence plus forecast data. Evidence strength hinges on elicited forecasts and normative choices; limited empirical validation. Uncertainty and break-even conditions are characterized well.

Coherent expected-utility framework with explicit parameters and extensive sensitivity analyses (timing of perils, extinction, risk-reducing science, race-to-safety). Assumptions are stated and explored. No preregistration; parameters partly speculative; robustness to alternative utility/discounting only partly addressed.

Quantifies the science-versus-risk tradeoff and offers decision thresholds; integrates metascience and biosecurity insights. Likely to inform funders and prioritization and moves discourse beyond qualitative debate.
Clear structure and goals; explicit assumptions and logical steps; conclusions match model outputs; decision-relevant thresholds communicated. Some risk of overreliance on forecast-driven results.
Uses public forecast data and is transparent about parameters. Unclear if full replication package/code is released; no preregistration; reproduction may require bespoke implementation.

Directly addresses high-stakes global priorities (returns to science, biosecurity, existential risk). Provides policy-relevant thresholds and comparative ROI useful to decision-makers and metascience strategy.

Overall reflects strong, policy-relevant synthesis with careful methods and transparent caveats, offset by reliance on observational studies and unclear openness. Score equals the rounded mean of component midpoints.

Clear central question; main quantitative claims are anchored in a systematic review/meta-analysis with publication-bias adjustments. Authors explicitly note non-experimental limits, explore unobserved confounding, and triangulate with natural experiments. Claims about learning-gap share and policy impacts are cautious and quantified.

Appropriate meta-analytic approach: structured search, harmonization, re-expression of coefficients, random-effects/meta-regression, publication-bias adjustments, and sensitivity to unobserved confounding. Limitations remain: observational base, potential residual confounding, heterogeneity, and small natural experiment set; preregistration/multiplicity controls unclear.

Provides an updated LMIC-focused effect size, reconciles heterogeneous literature, and quantifies contribution to global learning gaps. Offers decision-relevant elasticities and simulations useful to funders and policymakers. Adds nuanced comparisons to prior reviews and highlights priority populations for targeted interventions.

Objectives and assumptions are explicit; reasoning is transparent with clear derivations for re-scaling and bias adjustments. Narrative links evidence to conclusions and policy simulations. Writing and structure facilitate understanding; conclusions align with presented evidence and caveats.

Methods and data sources are described, but availability of full extraction datasets, analysis code, and preregistration is unclear from the provided text. Replicability likely feasible if materials are shared; uncertainty warrants a wide interval.

Topic is highly salient for LMIC health and education. Estimates directly inform regulation, remediation, and clinical/policy prioritization. Communication of magnitudes (SD gains) is actionable for decision-makers; simulations map to real interventions and target populations.

Strong causal design combining lab and field shows short-term, sizable effects and decay; clear heterogeneity. Some limits: student sample, small N (COVID), outcome restricted to canteen purchases, privacy-restricted data. Overall score reflects balanced strength across criteria.

Main questions are explicit; claims align with evidence. Causal identification via randomized price/WTP with IPW is persuasive; lab–field replication strong. Exploratory mechanisms are labeled as such. Limits: narrow population, context-specific video, outcomes exclude off-canteen consumption.

Innovative use of incentivized WTP to randomize exposure; IPW with known propensities; preregistration; robustness checks and placebo windows. Reasonable assumptions. Constraints: reduced sample, possible meal misclassification, limited external validity, potential residual confounds in field behavior.

Provides rare field-based causal evidence on willful ignorance’s behavioral consequences and decay; clarifies heterogeneity (avoiders vs seekers); informs intervention design and cost-effectiveness. Contributions are meaningful but bounded by domain, sample, and short-lived effects.

Clear writing, transparent logic, well-defined constructs, and thorough appendices. Figures and tables support arguments; limitations discussed. Minor complexity (bin pooling, multiple windows) could be streamlined further.

Pre-registered (AEARCTR), IRB-approved, detailed materials and appendices; VR content public. Likely data-sharing limits due to privacy; code availability not clearly stated. Replication feasible in principle with access to canteen data.

Relevant to animal welfare, climate, and design of information campaigns broadly. Practical insight: target avoiders; expect decay. External validity beyond students and meat context uncertain; effects short-lived and cost-effectiveness modest.

Overall quality is strong: a randomized program with careful analysis, clear writing, and high policy relevance. Limits include partial generalizability, inability to unbundle components, and moderate openness. The score is the rounded mean of the six category midpoints.

Clear questions and claims; evidence aligns well. Randomized assignment within PDSS plus DiD/event-study supports causal claims for the bundle. Auxiliary outside-group analyses are correlational and presented cautiously. Authors appropriately note context limits and mechanisms inferred via interviews and quality-scores, not experimental decomposition.

Strong design: randomized assignment, DiD with unit and time FE, event-time plots, block-bootstrapped SEs, multiple-testing adjustments, WLS for ratios, and contamination checks. Heterogeneity and mechanism probes add credibility. Limitations: no preregistration, imperfect ability to separate components, and non-causal matched comparisons.

Advances governance/PBF literature by demonstrating complementarities of incentives with auditing and feedback in LMIC non-profits, with sizable efficiency and mortality effects. Offers practical insight on funding vs governance. Generalizability and inability to isolate components temper the contribution.

Well-structured and transparent. Assumptions, context, design, and equations are clearly explained; results are linked to claims with appropriate caveats. Good discussion of alternative explanations and limitations. Minor complexity remains around mechanism inference.

Methods are described in detail and a data appendix exists, but underlying administrative data/interview data are likely restricted; replication materials and preregistration are not clearly provided. Transparency is reasonable; full reproducibility appears limited.

Highly relevant to LMIC health systems, donors, and ministries. Addresses SDG-aligned outcomes with actionable insights (governance plus A&F). Policy implications are clear; effects on mortality and efficiency are quantified. Findings are timely and decision-useful.

High-quality, policy-relevant multi-arm RCT with strong design and careful inference. Cash effects are robust; PM+ nulls are well-characterized. Communication is excellent. Open-science practices are good (pre-registration) but data/code availability is unclear, slightly lowering the aggregate. Overall equals mean of category midpoints.

Clear questions; multi-arm randomized design targets them directly. Evidence is strong for cash, null for PM+, and authors characterize findings cautiously. They probe alternative explanations (power, demand, timing) and add Bayesian framing for nulls. Some reliance on self-reports remains, though mitigated by envelope/smiley tasks.

Large, pre-registered cluster RCT with ANCOVA, stratification, spillover arms, FDR correction, power analysis, heterogeneity, timing analyses, and demand-effect test. Low attrition and good balance. Minor limitations: reliance on self-reports, no very-short-run endline, and many outcomes increase multiple-testing burden.

Head-to-head test of cash vs. psychotherapy at 1-year horizon in LMICs fills a key gap; robust cash effects, well-evidenced nulls for PM+, and cost comparisons inform prioritization. Provides thresholds for PM+ cost-effectiveness and insights on transfer frequency. Valuable for research and practice.

Argumentation is clear and transparent; assumptions and limitations are explicit. Results are tied carefully to claims; visuals and structure aid comprehension. Discussion thoughtfully situates findings within literature and policy without overreach.

Strong pre-registration and detailed methods enhance reproducibility; data integrity checks are documented. However, availability of analysis code and de-identified data is not clearly stated, limiting full reproducibility. Appendices are useful, suggesting above-median but not top-tier openness.

Directly relevant to global poverty and mental health policy. Quantifies economic and psychological impacts and compares costs, offering actionable insights for donors and implementers in LMICs. Findings are readily interpretable for policymakers.

Default equals mean of category midpoints. Strong large-scale, multi-domain evidence with clear framing and policy relevance. Main caveats are causality limits (citation-based impact, selection into pivots), possible construct validity issues in the pivot metric, and unknowns about code/data release. Nonetheless, findings appear robust and consequential.

Claims are clear (pervasive, growing pivot penalty; weak outsider advantage). Evidence spans millions of papers/patents, cross-fields, and event studies (COVID, push shocks). Strength stems from within-author analyses and broad consistency. Limits: impact proxied by citations, residual confounding/selection, and strong language (“nearly universal”) may outpace causal identification.

Pivot metric (1−cosine similarity of reference-journal or CPC distributions) is reasonable and scalable; within-person comparisons and multiple contexts bolster robustness. Likely extensive sensitivity checks. Remaining risks: measurement error in topic distance, audience/reputation channels, field/time normalization of citations, and potential multiple-testing concerns across many cuts.

Introduces a generalizable pivot measure and documents a large, growing penalty across science and technology, challenging common outsider/novelty narratives. Integrates shocks (COVID) to probe adaptability. Offers actionable implications for careers, funding, and organizational strategy. High incremental value to science-of-science and innovation policy.

Goals and constructs are well defined; reasoning is transparent; metric and intuition are clearly laid out. Narrative links evidence to claims coherently, with appropriate caveats noted. Minor risk of occasional overgeneralization and the usual complexity of field/period controls that can be hard to follow without appendices.

Scale suggests reproducible pipelines; patents/Dimensions are accessible, though Dimensions is partly restricted. Code/data availability is uncertain from the excerpt; likely partial release (common in this group), but full replication may require licensed data. Clarity of methods appears good; full computational reproducibility depends on shared code and documentation.

Directly relevant to policy on funding, crisis response (COVID case), and strategic specialization vs exploration across domains (health, climate, tech). Offers quantified, general patterns; less direct on cost-effectiveness or implementation playbooks, but highly informative for portfolio and talent management at agencies and institutions.

Strong RCT with clear, policy-relevant findings; robust evidence using both administrative monitoring and remote sensing; thoughtful cost-effectiveness. Some methodological caveats (self-initiated monitoring, RS labeling/training asymmetries, endline attrition) temper confidence slightly. Overall reflects mean of component scores.

Main questions are clear; claims tightly tied to experimental evidence. Consistent treatment effects across compliance and satellite-based outcomes; cost-effectiveness contextualized. Authors accurately characterize limitations (threshold sensitivity, potential inframarginality, monitoring reliance). Some reliance on treatment-group labels for RS negatives and self-requested verification modestly weakens evidentiary strength.

Clustered RCT with stratification; pre-analysis plan; appropriate inference (clustering, Lee bounds); well-motivated ML remote sensing with validation. Credible cost-effectiveness setup. Limitations: farmer-initiated monitoring may induce selection; RS model uses negatives from treatment only; heterogeneity analyses underpowered; some design features (caps, timing) constrain external validity.

Novel, policy-relevant test of PES contract timing for pollution abatement; first rigorous comparison for crop-residue burning. Demonstrates that partial upfront payments can outperform standard PES, informing contract design in LMICs. Provides actionable magnitudes for additionality and costs, advancing both PES and air-pollution control literatures.

Clear motivation, transparent reasoning, and consistent linkage between hypotheses, design, and results. Assumptions and tradeoffs (RS thresholds, compliance definition) are explicit. Presentation is careful; minor complexity around RS thresholding could challenge some readers but is handled responsibly.

AEARCTR preregistration; clear methods; appendices detail RS model and protocols. As a working paper, public code/data availability is unclear; RS inputs partly proprietary (Planet), limiting full replication. Likely reproducible with provided descriptions, but not yet exemplary on data/code release.

Addresses a major health and environmental externality in India with global analogs. Estimates substantial cost-effectiveness relative to alternatives (e.g., scrubbers). Findings are directly actionable for policymakers and implementers; scalability considerations are discussed. High practical importance for climate and air-quality policy.
Arithmetic mean of sub-scores. Strong clarity and exceptional global relevance are offset by modest methodological depth and limited open-science artifacts for a short P&P piece.

Questions and claims are clear; evidence blends theory, program facts, and suggestive comparisons. Authors are candid about counterfactual uncertainty and avoid over-claiming. Limited causal identification and reliance on external estimates constrain strength.

Sound theoretical framing (holdup/capacity) and reasonable assumptions for design questions. Empirical content is descriptive; no preregistration or robustness checks. Appropriate for a synthesis note but not a rigorous causal study.

Useful synthesis of AMC theory with practical design insights (capacity-linked subsidies, asymmetric loss). Incremental relative to prior work and pilot documentation, but policy-relevant and informative for future AMCs.
Clear, tightly argued, and well-caveated. Assumptions explicit; conclusions align with presented evidence. Accessible to policymakers; coherent link from theory to design and experience.
Cites public sources and provides clear factual references, but no new data or code; limited reusable materials. Replicability needs are modest given the format, yet transparency could be stronger.

Directly addresses high-priority global health policy with concrete implications for lifesaving interventions and procurement design. Actionable insights for donors and governments; high practical usefulness.

Arithmetic mean of other six midpoints. Strong, policy-relevant synthesis with robust analyses and clear conclusions; slight deductions for data/code availability and residual uncertainties about heterogeneity and moderators.

Clear primary claim (water treatment reduces U5 mortality) supported by pooled RCT evidence; both frequentist and Bayesian estimates; extensive sensitivity checks; publication-bias tests; predictive effects for new settings; conservative alternative model discussed. Claims are proportionate and limitations explicit.

Pre-registered PRISMA review; appropriate rare-event handling; random-effects and Bayesian models; clustering accounted for; meta-regression; broad sensitivity analyses. Constraints: limited power for moderators, reliance on some non-public author data, and unavoidable heterogeneity. OR choice reasonable; RR explored indirectly.

Delivers credible pooled RCT estimate of mortality effects long missing in WASH, shifting focus from diarrhea proxies to mortality. Coupled with careful cost-effectiveness across delivery models, it substantially affects prioritization and funding decisions.

Well-structured argument; assumptions, models, and limitations are explicit; figures/tables align with narrative; predictive vs mean effects clearly distinguished; policy implications clearly communicated. Some density typical of a working paper.

AEA registration and PRISMA compliance; substantial supplementary detail. However, full analysis code and harmonized datasets do not appear publicly archived; several inputs are author-provided and not easily reusable, limiting turnkey replication.

Directly targets a major global health burden with scalable interventions; provides DALY and net-benefit estimates, thresholds, and delivery options (dispensers, inline, MCH). Highly actionable for LMIC policymakers and funders.

Overall reflects solid quasi-experimental design and policy relevance, tempered by measurement limits (online auctions only), short post-period, and partially ad hoc substitute selection. Set to the rounded mean of other categories.

Clear main claim; SDID on 10-year panel with sensitivity/placebo tests supports positive spillovers. Evidence limited by single-year post period, reliance on one platform, imperfect substitutability assignment, and incomplete species identification among controls. Price effects not causally estimated.

Appropriate use of SDID with seasonality controls and announcement-period exclusion; robustness and placebo checks add credibility. Risks: short post window, measurement error from NLP classification, potential residual confounding, and no multiple-testing adjustment across taxa.

Makes a timely, policy-relevant contribution by quantifying spillovers to unregulated species using causal inference in conservation trade. Extends focus beyond banned species; generalizable insight despite Japan-specific setting.

Questions and conclusions are clearly stated; reasoning is mostly transparent and consistent with results. Minor gaps include limited elaboration of mechanisms and some brevity on data processing details.

Data source is public and methods described; SI reportedly includes datasets. However, no explicit code repository or full reproducible pipeline is cited; some controls lack species-level IDs, hindering full replication.

Highly relevant to wildlife-trade policy and biodiversity priorities; insights on unintended consequences and monitoring are actionable. Lacks quantified cost-benefit and cross-platform validation; external validity outside Japan is plausible but unproven.

Arithmetic mean of component scores. Strong causal evidence and contribution counterbalanced by residual concerns on spatial scale, sampling representativeness, and unclear replication package availability.

Clear questions; multiple complementary designs (panel FE, defense shift–share, upwind pollution IV, CAA policy). Effects are plausible, heterogeneous, and mechanisms partially quantified. Limitations (BioTIME representativeness, scale mismatch) acknowledged; claims mostly calibrated to evidence.

Reasonable and well-justified designs: FE panels, standard shift–share for military shocks, transported pollution IV, and regulatory DiD. Robustness appears broad. Residual risks: shift–share exposure endogeneity, site–state scale mismatch, sampling effort/detection biases, and multiple testing.

Large, multi-taxa biodiversity panel brought into economics; first broad causal estimates of GDP impacts; quantifies air pollution channel and shows regulatory mitigation and protected areas relevance. High value for macro–environment linkages and parameters for future work.

Goals and assumptions explicit; reasoning and limitations transparent; conclusions align with presented evidence. Complex channel decomposition is generally clear but could be streamlined further for non-specialists.

Relies on public datasets (BioTIME, pollution, regulations). However, the excerpt does not confirm full replication materials. Replicability hinges on releasing compiled data processing, site-level measures, and code with clear documentation.

US-focused but mechanisms generalize. Policy relevance high (pollution regulation co-benefits, protected areas). Useful elasticities provided; less emphasis on cost–benefit or implementation details. Informative for global biodiversity and environmental-economic policy.

High-quality, timely expert survey with preregistration and open materials. Clear claims backed by descriptive evidence; strong communication and practical relevance. Main limitations are purposive sampling, modest N, and limited generalizability. Overall equals the arithmetic mean of category midpoints.

Main claims are descriptive and closely match the data. Uncertainty and limitations are stated; no major overreach. Statistics and item-level results are reported transparently with appropriate caveats.

Purposive sampling (51/92 responses), Likert items, nonparametric tests with Holm-Bonferroni, preregistered plan largely followed. Reasonable for the questions, but selection/self-selection bias, small subgroup Ns, optional items reducing n, and limited representativeness constrain validity.

Synthesizes expert consensus on 50 practices, providing a useful foundation for standards, audits, and risk management. Adds structured priorities more than novel theory; actionable for labs and policymakers.
Clear goals, definitions, and argumentation; results aligned with conclusions. Figures/tables are informative; limitations and deviations from the PAP are explicit. Easy to follow throughout.
Pre-registration, pre-analysis plan, code, and data on OSF; deviations documented. Some data withheld to protect anonymity, but replication is still highly feasible.

Directly informs AGI lab practices and emerging policy (US/EU/UK). Timely and practically useful. Generalizability limited by expert sample composition and focus, but relevance to global AI governance is high.

A strong theoretical contribution with clear propositions, useful decomposition (state vs transition risk), and a policy layer yielding an x-risk Kuznets curve. Methods and logic are solid; relevance is high. Main uncertainty stems from empirical calibrations, stylized assumptions (planner, isoelastic utility, 1D technology), and unknown magnitude of policy frictions. Overall = mean of sub-scores.

Claims are clearly framed as positive (not normative). Evidence is theoretical: formal models, propositions, and proofs. Scope conditions and limitations are articulated. No empirical validation or calibration; depends on stylized assumptions. Good characterization of what follows under different γ and policy regimes.

Careful formal modeling; explores multiple regimes (state/transition risk, accrued stock, optimal policy, frictions). Clear first-order conditions and comparative statics; proofs promised in appendices. Assumptions (one-dimensional tech, representative planner, η>1) limit realism but are standard and justified for purpose.

Advances the literature by challenging ‘stagnation is safe,’ distinguishing state vs transition risk, deriving risk-minimizing growth, and introducing an existential-risk Kuznets curve. Likely to influence debates on growth, AI risk, and policy priorities; provides conditions guiding future empirical/theoretical work.

Reasoning is transparent; assumptions explicit; logical steps clear. Definitions and notation are consistent; diagrams aid intuition. Dense and technical at times; accessibility for non-specialists is limited but acceptable for a theory paper.

Derivations and proofs indicated; simulations documented with code in Appendix C; no proprietary data. Methods appear replicable. No preregistration (not expected for theory). Score depends on actual code availability and documentation quality.

Directly addresses existential risk policy and growth—core to global priorities (AI, bio, climate). Offers decision-relevant conditions (γ, elasticities, policy frictions). Absent calibrated estimates, but provides a framework to guide practical prioritization and research agendas.

Strong causal design with unusually long follow-up and clear policy relevance. Some uncertainty remains around measurement (self-reported child deaths), mediation not causal, and external validity beyond high-prevalence settings. Midpoint equals mean of component midpoints.

Main claim (22% U5MR reduction) is clearly stated, statistically supported, and robust across LPM/logit/probit and weights; IMR null appropriately noted. Dose-response strengthens credibility. Mechanism claims are carefully framed as exploratory correlations, not causal mediation, with limitations acknowledged.

Leverages randomized phase-in, high tracking, appropriate clustering and FE, prespecified analyses, and multiple robustness checks. Sensible handling of cross-cutting experiments. Limitations: parent-reported mortality and miscarriages, limited multiple-testing adjustments for many secondary outcomes, and non-causal mediation; possible assortative marriage effects.

Rare intergenerational experimental evidence from SSA on a major health program; large, policy-relevant effect sizes; links adolescent health to next-generation survival and informs cost-effectiveness parameters. Substantially advances debates on deworming externalities and long-run benefits.

Clear research questions, transparent exposition, and well-labeled results. Assumptions and limitations are stated (e.g., no formal mediation). Reasoning aligns with presented evidence; heterogeneity and mechanism sections are cautious. Dense in places but generally easy to follow.

Pre-registered (AEA registry), extensive appendices, and clear methods. Likely data access constraints due to confidentiality; full public replication materials are not fully evident from the WP text. Credible replication feasible with data access, but not turnkey open dataset/code.

Addresses child mortality in LMICs and a widely implemented intervention (school deworming). Quantified effects and IRR are directly useful for policymakers. External validity strongest where helminth prevalence is high; nonetheless highly relevant to global health priorities.
